table.text: The study was reviewed and approved by the institutional Research Ethics Committee at the Department of Psychology in Wrocław, SWPS University; ethics approval reference: 01/E/03/2026.
The study was conducted in line with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Eligible physicians worked in primary care in Poland for 6+ months and were recruited via professional networks and social media.
At the start of the survey, respondents received study information and provided informed consent.
We recruited a diverse sample that broadly resembled national patterns (e.g., high proportions of family medicine specialists, women, and those working in publicly funded clinics, Supplement 4).
Respondents gave informed consent before entering the anonymous online survey.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Strategies for Optimising Antibiotic Prescribing in Polish Primary Healthcare: A Survey with Physicians
table.research_questions:
This is a descriptive, exploratory survey study. No directional hypotheses are specified.

The study aims to examine physicians’ awareness, use, perceived competence, perceived impact and prioritization of antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) strategies in Polish primary healthcare, as well as perceived barriers and facilitators to their implementation. 

The research objectives are to:

Examine physicians’ use or awareness of AMS strategies (what strategies do they currently use/are aware of? Which strategies do they have access to?)
Examine physicians’ self-reported competencies regarding the use of AMS strategies (how competent do they consider (hypothetically) using the strategies?) 
Examine physicians’ perceived impact/efficacy of AMS strategies (how efficacious/effective do they perceive the AMS strategies to (hypothetically) be?)
Explore barriers and enablers to using AMS strategies in primary care (what impedes and enables the use of AMS strategies?)
Identify priority AMS strategies for implementation (what strategies should be implemented to enhance AMS in Polish primary care?)

Secondary objective:
Explore associations between physicians’ characteristics, their perceived importance of and role in AMS, and their use, competence and views on the impact of AMS strategies.

table.study_type: Non-randomized study: Does not include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes correlational studies, observational studies, surveys, natural experiments, real-world evidence studies, regression discontinuity designs, and descriptive studies.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: No causal relationship inferred: This study is not intended to inform a causal relationship.
table.study_design_overview:
This study is an observational, exploratory survey study using a cross-sectional design. 

The study will be conducted among physicians providing patient care in primary healthcare (general practice, “POZ”) settings in Poland. The target sample size is N=199. A convenience sampling approach will be used, with recruitment via professional and academic networks. Participation will be voluntary and anonymous.

Data will be collected primarily via an online questionnaire (CAWI), with telephone interviews (CATI) used if needed as a supplementary method. No intervention will be applied. The survey will include approximately 20 items and will take about 10 minutes to complete. It will assess physicians’ views and practices regarding AMS strategies and collect basic professional characteristics.
table.data_collection_procedures:
POPULATION: Physicians practising in general practice (“POZ”) in Poland for at least 6 months, fluent in Polish. 

RECRUITMENT: Participants will be recruited through professional networks via the Polish Society of Family Medicine (“Polskie Towarzystwo Medycyny Rodzinnej, PTMR”) (e.g., via newsletters, social media), professional/academic networks of the research team, and potentially (if needed) an external social/marketing research agency. 

METHOD: Data will be collected primarily using an online questionnaire via the Qualtrics platform. Optionally, Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviews (CATI) may be used if needed to reach the planned sample size.  

INCENTIVES/REIMBURSEMENTS: None.
table.sample_size: The target sample size is N=199.
table.sample_size_rationale: The target sample size at N=199 was estimated for regression analyses based on the detection of medium-sized effects (0,15) in a model including 15 potential predictors.
table.measured_variables:
The questionnaire (approx. 20 items) will measure: 
Respondents characteristics: Professional specialty/training, years of practice, type of practice (public/private).
Attitudes: Perceived importance of AMS, perceived role/responsibility in AMS, perceived risk of AMR.
AMS Strategies Assessment: For various strategies (e.g., Guidelines, Education, Media campaigns), the survey will measure: 
Awareness or use of the strategy
Perceived competence in using the strategy
table.statistical_tests:
1. Descriptive analyses will be used to address Objectives 1-4 (describing respondent characteristics and AMS-related awareness, competence, impact, and barriers).
2. Correlation/Regression analyses will be used for the secondary objective (Objective 6) to explore associations between physicians characteristics/attitudes and their views on AMS strategies.
table.inference_criteria: Standard criteria (e.g., p<0.5) will be used for statistical significance in regression/correlational analyses.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Participants will be included if they are practising primary care physicians in Poland (≥6 months), fluent in Polish, and provide informed consent. Responses not meeting inclusion criteria, lacking consent, or duplicate entries will be excluded. No formal outlier exclusion will be applied; all valid data will be analysed.
table.missing_data_handling: Analyses will be conducted on all available data.

report: #### Repositories that could not be checked

These repositories are linked in the paper, but their contents could not be retrieved, so nothing below describes them. When the reason is that the platform did not answer, running the check again later may work.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Repository = "osf.io/a4r9k", Platform = "osf", Error = "closed registration source", "All Files" = 0L, "Data Files" = 0L, "Code Files" = 0L, READMEs = 0L, Archives = 0L), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE) ```
README files were found in all repositories.

#### Registration Points to a Closed Project

1 OSF project (https://osf.io/a4r9k) is referenced by a registration in this manuscript, but it is closed or inaccessible, and no copy of its files could be found anywhere else. Some OSF registrations only describe what was shared, while the actual files live in the project they were registered from — if that project is closed and the registration holds no copy, metacheck cannot list or download its files, and other researchers cannot access them either. Consider making the source project openly available, or re-uploading its files directly into the registration.
